title: From Pen-and-Paper to AI in Two Generations - The Wire China
gist: A profile of Guo Ruize, who joined his father's laser-cutting factory in Shenyang in 2016 when it was run from a paper clipboard, which frames how small Chinese manufacturers are jumping from pen-and-paper management straight to AI within one family's succession. This is a paywalled teaser.

themes.theme: Leapfrog digitization of Chinese SME factories

insights.claim: As recently as 2016, a laser-cutting factory in Shenyang managed its production schedule with a clipboard hung on a workshop wall, with managers scribbling handwritten changes as new orders arrived.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Many Chinese small manufacturers start from a very low digital base, so the addressable market for industrial software and AI scheduling tools is large.
insights.quote: A clipboard hung on a workshop wall. Managers would grab it to scribble handwritten changes to the production schedule as new orders came in.

insights.claim: Generational succession in Chinese family factories, with engineering-trained children taking over, is a channel through which small manufacturers move from paper-based management straight to AI tools.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Succession timing in China's SME base is a demand driver for AI and industrial SaaS adoption; watch vendors that sell to small job-shop manufacturers.

insights.claim: Job-shop factories that cut materials into sheets for clients across many industries face constantly changing orders, which makes production scheduling a natural early use case for AI.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: High-mix, low-volume Chinese manufacturers are where AI scheduling may add the most productivity, which reinforces China's cost advantage in fabrication.
